title: Cycle Detection Check
description: Predict Floyd's tortoise-and-hare behavior on next-pointer chains.

questions.prompt: In Floyd's algorithm, how many steps does the `fast` pointer take for every one step of `slow`?

options.text: The same one step
Two steps
Three steps
It depends on the list length

questions.explanation: `fast` always moves two steps (`next[next[fast]]`) while `slow` moves one step (`next[slow]`) — the differing speed is what causes them to meet inside a cycle.

questions.prompt: For `next = [1, 2, 3, 1]` starting at index `0` (chain `0 -> 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 1 -> ...`), does `hasCycle` return `true` or `false`?

options.text: `true` — `slow` and `fast` eventually land on the same index
`false` — `fast` reaches `-1` first
It throws an error
It runs forever without returning

questions.explanation: The chain loops back to index `1`, so it has a cycle. Because `fast` never reaches `-1` (it just keeps looping), `slow` and `fast` are guaranteed to meet.

questions.prompt: For `next = [1, 2, -1]` starting at index `0` (chain `0 -> 1 -> 2 -> end`), what happens?

options.text: `hasCycle` returns `true`
`hasCycle` returns `false` because `fast` reaches `-1`
It throws because `fast` goes out of bounds
`slow` and `fast` meet at index `2`

questions.explanation: The chain ends cleanly (no cycle). Since the loop condition checks `fast !== -1 && next[fast] !== -1`, it stops before dereferencing an invalid index, and returns `false`.

questions.prompt: Compared to the hash-set approach, what does Floyd's tortoise-and-hare trade away to save memory?

options.text: It becomes `O(n^2)` time
It uses two pointers instead of a `Set`, still `O(n)` time but `O(1)` extra space
It only works on arrays, not linked lists
It cannot detect cycles at all, only measure length

questions.explanation: Floyd's algorithm keeps the same `O(n)` time complexity as the hash-set version but uses `O(1)` extra space instead of `O(n)` for a `Set`.

questions.prompt: For `next = [2, 2, 2]` starting at index `0`, is there a cycle?

options.text: No — the chain ends at `-1`
Yes — node `2` points to itself, forming a self-loop
It depends on the starting index
Cycles require at least 4 nodes

questions.explanation: `0 -> 2 -> 2 -> 2 -> ...` — node `2`'s `next` points to itself, which is a valid (and detectable) cycle even though it involves just one node looping.

questions.prompt: Does a 'cycle' in this context require looping back to the very first node visited?

options.text: Yes, only a loop back to the start counts
No — any node's `next` chain revisiting an earlier node counts as a cycle
Yes, but only for arrays of even length
No — a cycle must visit every node in the list

questions.explanation: A cycle exists whenever the chain of `next` pointers revisits any node already seen, not necessarily the very first one — as in `0 -> 1 -> 2 -> 1 -> ...`.
